title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 7
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all 40 questions.

passages.title: The Buried Achievement
passages.text:
A. Of the interventions that lengthened human life in industrialising cities, the one with the largest measured effect was not a treatment. It was the separation of drinking water from waste. Historians of medicine comparing mortality decline against the introduction of therapies have consistently found that most of the improvement preceded effective drugs, and followed water supply and sewerage instead — a finding that is well established and sits awkwardly with how medical history is popularly told.

B. The obstacle to acting was not ignorance of the association. That crowded districts suffered worse epidemics had been observed for centuries. What was absent was a mechanism, and in its absence the dominant explanation held that disease arose from foul air. This theory was wrong and it was not stupid: it accounted for the association with filth, with low-lying ground and with heat, and it made a prediction — remove the smell and you remove the disease — that led to sanitary reforms which frequently worked, for reasons other than those given.

C. The decisive evidence was epidemiological rather than laboratory-based, and it was resisted. A London physician mapped cholera deaths against the water pumps that households used, and showed the cases clustered around one supply. Crucially, he identified households near the pump that escaped and traced their water elsewhere — the exceptions did more work than the pattern, since a cluster alone was equally consistent with foul air. Acceptance nonetheless took decades and arrived only when the organism was identified.

D. Building the infrastructure raised a problem that recurs in public works and is rarely stated plainly. Sewerage benefits everyone in a district including those who do not pay, and its cost falls on identifiable people in a single decade while the benefit accrues to others over a century. No private arrangement assembles that, which is why sanitation in almost every city was financed publicly and compulsorily, and why the argument for it was made in the language of morality when the underlying structure was economic.

E. The engineering choices made then constrain cities now in ways their designers could not have anticipated. Many systems combined foul water and rainwater in a single pipe, which was cheaper and worked adequately at the population densities and paved areas of the time. As cities grew and surfaces became impermeable, heavy rain began to exceed capacity, and the designed response — discharging the excess, untreated, into rivers — became routine rather than exceptional. Separating those flows now means rebuilding beneath established streets at a cost no municipality readily faces.

F. The global position is frequently misreported as a technical problem. Sanitation reaching everyone is not limited by unavailable engineering; the methods are old and well understood. It is limited by the same structure that operated in the nineteenth century — costs concentrated, benefits diffuse, and institutions required to collect from many to build something none of them will individually own. Where that structure has been solved, coverage followed; where it has not, coverage has stalled regardless of technical assistance.

passages.title: The Reef and Its Partner
passages.text:
A coral reef is built by an animal that cannot feed itself adequately. The coral polyp captures some plankton, but the great majority of its energy comes from single-celled algae living inside its own tissues, which photosynthesise and pass the products to their host. In exchange the algae receive shelter and nutrients. This partnership is what allows reefs to grow in tropical waters that are, in terms of dissolved nutrients, close to deserts.

Bleaching is the collapse of that partnership rather than the death of the coral. Under stress — most commonly water warmer than the local seasonal maximum, sustained for weeks — the coral expels its algae, losing both its colour and its principal food supply. A bleached coral is alive and starving. If conditions return to normal quickly enough, algae can be reacquired and the colony recovers; if not, it dies. This is why bleaching events are described in terms of duration and accumulated heat rather than peak temperature alone.

The recovery interval is where the trend matters more than any single event. Reefs have always experienced disturbance — storms, disease, occasional heat — and recover over years to decades if left alone. What has changed is frequency. Where severe bleaching recurs every few years, the interval falls below the recovery time, and the reef does not return to its previous state before being struck again. The mechanism of decline is therefore not that any one event is unsurvivable but that the gaps have closed.

Not all corals respond alike, and the differences are the basis of most current optimism and some overstatement. Fast-growing branching species are highly vulnerable and also recolonise quickly; massive slow-growing species resist heat better and replace far more slowly. Some colonies host algal strains with higher thermal tolerance, and there is evidence that populations exposed to variable temperatures bleach at higher thresholds. This is real and it is a shift of a degree or so, not an open-ended capacity to adapt, and the distinction is routinely lost in reporting.

Local pressures interact with heat in ways that make them worth addressing even though they are not the primary driver. Nutrient runoff favours algae that compete with coral for space; sediment reduces the light the symbionts need; overfishing of herbivorous species removes the grazing that keeps competing seaweed in check. A reef under these pressures bleaches at the same temperature as one that is not, and recovers less well afterwards. Local action does not stop bleaching and measurably changes what happens next.

Intervention proposals now range from assisted gene flow to shading and larval seeding, and their honest assessment is that none operates at the scale of the problem. A reef system spans hundreds of kilometres; the largest restoration projects cover a few hectares. This does not make them worthless — they preserve genetic material and refine methods — but presenting them as a solution rather than as preparation misrepresents both their purpose and their scale.

passages.title: Before Anaesthesia
passages.text:
Surgery before the 1840s was performed on conscious patients, and the constraint this imposed shaped the discipline more than any other factor. Operations had to be fast, because a patient could not be held still indefinitely and shock killed. The surgeons most admired were the quickest, and the range of possible procedures was limited to what could be reached and completed in minutes — essentially amputations and superficial work. Opening the abdomen or chest was not a technical impossibility so much as a practical one.

The compounds that would change this were known and used recreationally for decades before anyone applied them medically. Nitrous oxide and ether both produced insensibility and both featured in public demonstrations as entertainments. That the gap between recreational use and surgical application lasted so long is the part of the story that most repays attention: the observation that a person under these substances did not respond to injury was made repeatedly and not acted on, because pain was widely understood as a necessary accompaniment to healing rather than as a symptom to be removed.

The demonstrations that established surgical anaesthesia in the 1840s were followed by adoption of remarkable speed for the period — within a year the technique was in use across Europe — which itself indicates how strongly the constraint had been felt. Priority disputes among the several claimants were bitter, protracted and, for at least two of them, ruinous. The disputes matter historically less for who was right than for what they reveal: a technique with obvious commercial value emerged from a context where practitioners had assumed no such value existed.

The consequences were not straightforwardly beneficial in the short term. With time no longer limiting, surgeons attempted procedures previously impossible, and mortality in some categories rose sharply, because the barrier that had prevented those operations had also prevented the infections they produced. Anaesthesia made surgery survivable to perform and antisepsis, arriving decades later, made it survivable to receive. The interval between them is a period in which a genuine advance measurably increased deaths — an uncomfortable pattern that recurs whenever one constraint is removed while another remains.

Modern practice has inherited a question the early period could not pose. Anaesthesia is now understood to comprise several distinct effects — unconsciousness, immobility, suppression of the stress response, and prevention of memory formation — which are produced by different mechanisms and can be separated. A patient may be immobile and unaware but forming no memory while retaining some processing of the event. This makes the apparently simple question of whether a patient was conscious considerably harder to answer than it appears, and it is the reason depth of anaesthesia remains monitored rather than assumed.
